chief_complaint: hypertension in upper extremities, weak delayed femoral pulses, and systolic murmur across back in 8-year-old
hpi_details: 8-year-old boy noted to have right arm blood pressure 138/88 mmHg with diminished femoral pulses and radio-femoral pulse delay. Chest radiography shows inferior rib notching and a figure-3 sign, with echocardiography confirming aortic coarctation.
ideas: She thinks his high blood pressure might just be from nervousness at the doctor's office or eating too much salty food lately.
concerns: She is worried he might have a serious kidney problem or risk a stroke at a young age like his grandfather did.
expectations: She hopes to have his blood pressure rechecked while he is relaxed and receive guidance on dietary changes.

teaching.one_liner: 8-year-old boy with upper extremity hypertension, weak/delayed femoral pulses, and a systolic murmur heard over the back.
red_flags: Blood pressure discrepancy between arms and legs
Chest pain, severe headache, fainting, shortness of breath, or neurologic symptoms require emergency assessment

must_ask.objective: Ask about leg symptoms with exercise
must_ask.say: Does he ever complain of leg pain, cramping, or getting tired quickly during sports?

must_ask.objective: Ask about headaches or nosebleeds (hypertension symptoms)
must_ask.say: Has he had frequent headaches or nosebleeds?

must_ask.objective: Ask about growth and general health history
must_ask.say: How has his overall growth and energy level been?

must_ask.objective: Explain the pulse and blood pressure exam findings
must_ask.say: We found that his arm blood pressure is high and his leg pulses feel weaker and delayed compared to his arms — this points to a narrowing in his aorta.

must_ask.objective: Explain the cardiology referral and treatment plan
must_ask.say: We need to refer him to a pediatric cardiologist for imaging, and he'll likely need a procedure to open the narrowed part of the aorta.

history.answer: We're here because my son was told he had high blood pressure at a routine school physical.
Two days ago at school, the nurse checked his blood pressure and said it was 138 over 88, which is high for an eight-year-old.
His blood pressure was always completely normal at earlier checkups, so this is the very first time anyone noticed it.
He had been sitting quietly in the nurse's office, was not anxious, and had not been running around or feeling sick.
We do not own a blood pressure cuff at home, so we have not remeasured it ourselves.
He has had occasional dull headaches after school over the past month, but he does not seem unusually fatigued.
He often tells us that his legs feel tired, crampy, or cold when he runs around during soccer practice.
He has had nosebleeds every couple of weeks recently, usually stopping on their own after a few minutes.
He has never complained of chest tightness, chest pain, or trouble catching his breath.
He has not had any blurry vision, fainting spells, numbness, or weakness in his arms or legs.
His urination is completely normal with no pain or foamy urine, and his face and ankles have never looked puffy.
He does not get excessive sweating, heart pounding episodes, heat intolerance, or unusual thirst.
He has had no fever, night sweats, unexplained weight loss, or swollen glands.
He eats regular home-cooked meals, drinks mostly water and milk, and does not eat excessively salty snacks.
No one in our family smokes, and he has never been around cigarette smoke or dust.
He has never used steroid medications or inhalers, and he has never broken a bone.
He has never been exposed to anyone with tuberculosis and has never had a chronic cough.
I thought his blood pressure might just be high because he gets nervous at the doctor or has been eating too much salty junk food recently.
I'm terrified he might have a bad kidney problem or end up having a stroke like his grandfather did at a young age.
I'm hoping you can recheck his blood pressure while he is calm and tell us if we need to change his diet.
He has had no chronic medical illnesses and has always been a healthy child.
He has never had any operations and has never stayed overnight in a hospital.
He does not take any regular prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or vitamin supplements.
He has no known allergies to medicines, foods, or anything else.
He was born at full term via a normal vaginal delivery with no complications and a birth weight of 3.2 kilograms.
He has met all developmental milestones on time and his height and weight have always tracked along the 50th percentile.
All of his childhood immunizations are fully up to date.
He attends the second grade at our local elementary school and lives at home with both parents.
There is no family history of early heart disease, childhood high blood pressure, stroke, or kidney failure.
He is an eight-year-old child, so alcohol and recreational substances do not apply.

exam.finding: Right arm blood pressure is 138/88 mmHg, left arm blood pressure is 136/86 mmHg, and bilateral thigh blood pressures are 102/64 mmHg with heart rate 82 bpm, respiratory rate 18/min, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
An alert, well-developed, and well-nourished 8-year-old boy sitting comfortably with no signs of respiratory distress.
Height and weight are both at the 50th percentile for age with symmetric body proportions.
Upper extremity pulses are brisk and bounding bilaterally, while femoral and pedal pulses are markedly diminished with palpable radio-femoral delay.
Regular rate and rhythm with normal S1 and S2, accompanied by a grade 3/6 systolic ejection murmur heard best at the left upper sternal border and interscapular back.
Symmetric chest wall without visible collateral vessels, heaves, or thrills.
Clear breath sounds bilaterally throughout all lung fields without wheezing, crackles, or rhonchi.
Normal active bowel sounds present in all four quadrants with no epigastric or renal artery bruits audible.
Soft, non-tender, and non-distended abdomen with no guarding, rigidity, or palpable masses.
Liver and spleen are not palpable below the costal margins.
Thyroid gland is normal in size, non-tender, and smooth with no nodules or bruits.
No palpable anterior or posterior cervical lymphadenopathy.
Both lower extremities feel cool compared to the upper extremities, with a capillary refill time of three seconds and no peripheral edema.
